Also fuck this phrasing of pathological demand avoidance. It's only phrased that way because they saw a pattern in those not like them but couldn't see the patterns in all the fucking water they're swimming in all the time.

Pervasive Drive for Autonomy because the way current academia and scientific communities talk about it (traditional ones who aren't keeping up to date with what the actual community thinks) infantilizes people as if they can't make decisions on their own even when they might desire making those decisions. Every single person on this Earth experiences something they don't want to do and is capable of figuring out what is driving the avoidance that is perceived as pervasive. 

Categorizing and formalizing language and shared terms about a behavior shouldn't be the thing that enables others to empathize with my struggles. If it is, then I don't want it. Because clearly your empathy is still limited to a simplistic rule of if thing = human and care about human = good then I, a human, should care about thing. What about maybe thinking about the impact you're having on someone and if you don't think you can be responsible with the potential impact you will have on someone else, then remove yourself, you irresponsible bum???

I broke up with Joe because I couldn't handle the pain anymore. I couldn't handle how much his decisions were hurting me. And I definitely couldn't handle them continuing without any change to be seen on the horizon. That's enough. It doesn't have to be about characteristics of a person. It just needs to be about the behavior and the impact and if it can improved upon. 

At the end of the day, I wish he didn't tell me that he was okay with not having children. I wish he took the first few times I asked him in our relationship as a way to prevent pain. But he only thought about the future when it benefitted him and his legacy. God, this is such a waste of time. Writing this all down. Because I know how I feel about this. I had moments when I recognized his non-painful behavior. And maybe that was too much credit. 

I don't think I had high expectations for our relationship Joe. But honestly, even if that is the narrative you decided on, that's okay with me as long as you accepted that you couldn't meet them and you needed less expectations.

It pisses me off so much that Joe asked me to move back to New York City. 

1. He knew about all the painful experiences I had growing up there. 
2. He knew that I desperately did not want to travel to NYC for the holidays or for that matter, ever. 
3. I would have to argue about it every year when he kept trying to convince me to go to the holidays up until the last time I had it where I asked him why he couldn't tell his parents his decision without including me. 
4. He BARELY HAD A STABLE JOB after years of me supporting his living out here AFTER HE SPECIFICALLY ASKED TO COME OUT TO CALIFORNIA WITH ME. 
5. He knew that me healing from those painful experiences and my health was my number one priority. 
6. He didn't want to make any friends in a place where he's surrounded by like-minded people who are interested in the same things as he is. How would that change at ALL by moving to a city you know nothing about?
7. He has no relational awareness about anyone that is a part of his life nor does it exist when applied to even where he positions himself on any given street. He's always in the way not considering that he's on a crowded street. If it happens once, he doesn't learn from it to prevent it again. Then he gets angry at the person and the situation as if he's entitled to that space. 

There's nothing I wish more than to enjoy some of the places that were respite for me when growing up but not at the expense of having to share past pain with someone who I can't trust to even take careful consideration of current pain I'm going through. 

No wonder I started shoving things down and not saying anything anymore. I lost my sense of safety and trust in him the day he tried to fuck me while I was asleep. I lost it the day I was sick with a respiratory infection and he didn't help take care of me. I lost it the day he heard me say no to taking out the trash that night and tried to whittle me down into doing the dishes. I lost it when I planned co-op game nights and he would end up just solving everything by himself and not wait for me or include me and when I said something about it , he got defensive about his way of doing things. No matter how much space I tried to take in my own autonomy, he always saw it as a personal affront and the only reason why he would see it as a personal affront is if he viewed me something he is entitled to or he viewed his relationship with me as status that he was entitled to. 

Regardless of me perceiving any of that shit as a demand, I can say no to things and should have to feel forced into doing that thing. You can make a convincing argument and see if you can help me see the benefit. But specifically asking why I always have to ask about the why instead of just doing the thing is a sure fire way to lost my trust and any access to my vulnerability. 

I think he's a shit partner. I think he doesn't know how to be a good one no matter the person. I think he knows it's hard and because it feels hard, it makes him think it shouldn't be hard and he's entitled to ease. I think he'll continue to be a terrible partner. I think he'll be a terrible father. And funnily enough, the same amount of information I have now from to disprove any of those conclusions is the same fucking amount of information I had when I was in the relationship with him. Fuck him. At least, I know to take my time now with someone. And weed out people with this behavior. 

Regardless of whether identity is intrinsic or not, I am devoted to my mental health first because no one else is going to do that for me and no one else has ever done that for me. If there continues to be patterns in how I engage with a certain population of people and those patterns are more informed by the public's view on masculinity, sexuality, "perfect" relationships or taboo and unconventional ones, then I'm fine being an equal and opposite force to maintain the space I take up not only to live but to thrive.

Despite the emotional intensity, the thoughts remain connected and purposeful, with only minor sentence-level awkwardness rather than fragmentation or cognitive disorganization.

Jason still confuses me. He just wants to be around me. He tells me he misses me. He apologizes and works through miscommunication so he doesn't hurt me. Is this what it's like to date someone who actually likes you for who you are rather who you can be?

Ironically, now that Jason (and John) want to spend time with me, I feel more capable of being friends with Joe and offering emotional labor for him. I offered him to see Cocoa this week while I'm out in Finland. I thought connecting with him about stuff from the past. I guess, I don't thin that's a very good idea but he's intelligent and wants to talk about tech. Maybe that's what I can start with.

Today marks the first time I've ever taken a trip for leisure by myself. I've gone trips before by myself but they have always been for work. I'm so proud of myself because I booked everything, I got all the paperwork needed, I packed, I communicated, and I never felt stressed out by the airport part one bit. I happened upon the lounge this time instead of making it an itinerary item like Joe did in the past. I feel cautiously optimistic about this trip. I hope it is life changing. I want to write my wishes under the Northern Lights. Breaking up with Joe has been hard but it's gave me so much more self-confidence in my ability to handle life no matter the status of external support. I read something today about AI from Frank Chimero called Beyond The Machine. Near the end of the piece, there's an allegory painted into knowing when to place boundaries, when to determine "enough" and Chihuro's refusal to take anything that No Face offers her. At the end, he likens the act and discipline to how we need to work with AI and finalizing his argument with a quote from Simone Weil: "We have to endure the discordance between imagination and fact. It is better to say, ‘I am suffering,’ than to say, ‘This landscape is ugly.’” 

He continues to summarize with, "In other words, it is better to stay with your own experience instead of projecting it outward."

I need ways to practice this. In becoming more aligned to who I am and what I value, I need to focus on learning about myself and what my internal world is telling me about myself rather than projecting it onto an object or being that doesn't have that intention. 

The other day, I was starting up a game of RV There Yet? with a couple of new friends. One of them, Duke, is similar to me in that when a puzzle problem is presented, I want to approach it seriously and academically. I want to solve it even in partnership with others. But I also expect those who are with me to approach it in a similar way. When someone is having fun from the same experience in a completely different way, it's okay to me as long as it's not being imposed on me and taking away from presence and experience. The other two guys playing were not aligned with that at all and were trolling in how I would describe it. I think at the end of the day, I understood that there were multiple opinions flying at rapid succession at each other about what we should be doing and why someone did something that all came to head in triggering me. An actual real trigger. I started disassociating. I was a teenager again, cradling myself in my room, trying not to listen to my parents fight with each other again. And yet I was also aware that this wasn't reality. And the experience I was having internally was not happening with anyone else. In the end, I stopped. I was crying. I told them what was happening and what I needed. I was scared about them belittling my need. It didn't happen. It was an experience that I only had and none of them shared. I think at the end, the game had nothing to do with what happened. It wasn't the design of the game that caused. It might have contributed but there was no intention to trigger me. And at the same time, me, with my background and experiences, was triggered. 

I guess...it's maybe something for me to be aware of and try to learn to deal with in a more grounded way. I don't know if I'm ready for it. I do think that I need to make a goal for it though.

Contradictions are explicitly recognized and held together well—especially the distinction between external events and internal triggering—while minor hedging at the end slightly softens the otherwise organized, reflective narrative.

I was looking for Things that make me happy menu earlier today and coincidentally, searching for "happy" in my reflections brought me this one from a few days before my dad's funeral. 

I've been feeling aimless like I previously mentioned and I read through my reflection and cried really hard. I feel better after reading through it. I don't know where this thoughtful writer came from. And I wish I could harness it more at will rather than my environment and my relationship with my surroundings and interactions determining when it comes out. 

Here's the reflection from November 14th, 2023:

For a while during the pandemic, I started thinking about my dad’s death, his funeral, what life would be like after him. At the same time, I was conflicted with self-judgement about this morbidity and a generally negative view of how I felt that I’ve internalized from family over the years. 

I now know that my mind, body, and soul felt this way because I was already starting to grieve — to grieve the dad that loved me so much and unconditionally, that he wouldn’t ever hurt me, physically, mentally, and emotionally. I grieved the dad that pushed me to excel, to always look for improvement, and to witness my growth. I grieved the dad that understood others and seemed to always want to learn because he was curious even if it could be perceived as embarrassing. I grieved because I lost a person who was so foundational to how I viewed the world and others as complex beings and full of awe, just as he previously was.

As the years went by and I've grown older, I watched my dad become less and less multi-dimensional, to the point that anger, resentment, and abuse was all he had left to share. I watched as comparison and a false standard of normalcy ripped all of the empathy out of him and replaced it with unrelenting competition. I sat by his bedside in the hospital, year after year, seeing how our systems continually placed unnecessary burdens on him to figure things out. I held my tongue when he lashed out at those who loved him, who cared for him, and who offered help, because he didn’t know how to deal with vulnerability and feeling emotions so big that they changed the very core of his being. I continued to hope that he would remember how to choose kindness again. Others couldn’t see what my mom and I had seen in him anymore.

For better or for worse, he is one of the few people that is integral to who I am today, how I conduct myself today, and how I perceive the world and others. If anything, his changes signaled that I can’t let trauma sit and hope that it goes away. I must face it head on. I must break the cycle.

It might be easy to other yourself from his story and from anyone else who experiences life and behaves the way he did. But humans are so complex not only because of what we’re made of, but because of with whom and what we interact. I’m in my 7th year of therapy, of asking for help, advocating for my mental and emotional health, and learning how to be the most decent and kind version of myself.

Choosing kindness starts with you. Choosing to grow, find purpose, find happiness in your life is your responsibility. But it’s our collective responsibility that each one of us has the safety, agency, and easy access to make that choice. 

Whether it’s learning how to communicate non-violently or becoming more emotionally intelligent, whether it’s knowing how to soothe yourself or encouraging yourself to express how you’re feeling and what you need, whether it’s to ask for help and be proud of your vulnerability or acknowledge that you don't have it all figured out — growth requires a strong foundation to place roots in and constant nurturing.

By volunteering for mental health organizations, helping people understand how common of a human experience it is to struggle, advocating for better health care, educating yourself on the myriad of experiences marginalized folks go through, supporting the freedom to creatively express, you validate others to be complex and human and still kind. 

You offer help because you know how hard it was for you to struggle alone and you know how meaningful it would feel to have belonging and understand that you’re not alone. You offer help because you’ve forgiven the situation but have not forgotten. 

History weeps as it retraces the parabola.

The person who is always afraid someone's mad at them has often grown up focusing on others needs being met out of their survival. They were shamed for needing help. They got the silent treatment with no warning. They're on high alert deeply hoping not to get hurt like that again.

Having cPTSD is like living in an echo chamber but when you scream, it echoes back the words of all the people who've abused you, lied to you, manipulated you. It's blindly trusting that each step taken to heal will one day help you hear your own voice again.

Grief in healing comes with pressure that feels like you're losing time. That reaction is from remembering past events you didn't know you'd have to heal from later. We want time to pause so we can catch up. Trust, you're not losing time — you're gaining truth. Peace is coming.

Many people are born into systems that forced them to be in survival mode. Years later, they'll begin to understand that their minds & bodies have to work harder to function because of this. I can't think of anyone who deserves understanding more than someone who knows this pain.

You'll be treated poorly by people threatened by your growth. They won't see your heartache. They won't see your lonely nights. They won't respect what you've fought for because their inner world is about pulling people into their pain rather than witnessing someone heal theirs.

It it confusing to experience abuse from those who say they love us. It makes love scary and often convinces us that isolation is safer than exposure to similar pain. Healing comes from naming: 1. That was abuse, not love. 2. You are only meant for love.

Those who've had to fight for their healing have a strong reaction to inauthenticity. People blame them for being too much, when it's really because there's not enough truth around them. Not enough resources. Not enough honesty around systems that keep people oppressed.

The least likely people to pass down generational trauma are the ones self-aware enough to be afraid they will.

"Are you happy?" "In all honesty? No. But I am curious — I am curious in my sadness, and I am curious in my joy. I am everseeking, everfeeling. I am in awe of the beautiful moments life gives us, and I am in awe of the difficult ones. I am transfixed by grief, by growth. It is all so stunning, so rich, and I will never convince myself that I cannot be somber, cannot be hurt, cannot be overjoyed. I want to feel it all — I don't want to cover it up or numb it. So no, I am not happy. I am open, and I wouldn't have it any other way."

Nothing has shaped my life like Grief has. So when people say "When will you get over it", my answer is "I hope never". Nothing has helped shape my life around living and who and what matters most to me more than the reality of how short it all is. And how much I want to be me. While there's still time...

"If John and my relationship is severed because he needs to prioritize Erin, I hope it's on amicable terms because I don't want to lose a person to go to kink parties with." That fear though might be holding me back from the level of agency I want in my relationships. 

I've previously wondered out loud if I should move to San Francisco so that I'm closer to the scene up there. John responded with a hesitating pause, after which he said "Don't move any further away from me" while patting my left leg and knee. It felt a little infantilizing to me. And it's been bothering me ever since. In the beginning of our blooming friendship, I found myself very honest with him. This was when I was still in a relationship with Joe. Now I'm not and I'm also having a hard time being upfront with him about what I'm feeling because I don't think it's his responsibility to care in that way. I do recall feeling similarly to this before with Luke, but where I was projecting that on him for why he kept isolating himself. I can feel as John asks more questions of me, I give shorter and shorter answers so as to not reveal myself too much. 

So something has occurred. Maybe it's from the play over Folsom weekend where we engaged in a little bit of torment of me and the after care was not enough for me to not make up narratives about how he might manipulate me or influence me to make certain kinds of decisions. There's definitely some kind of fear here. 

On top of all of this, I'm pretty sure I've contracted mono, which, although everything online days most people have the contributing bits in their body in a dormant state, has really crushed me for some reason. The grossness of the white striations on my tonsils are amplifying this feeling. I think I also am uncomfortable with the ambiguity of how to manage and treat it since all I was able to do yesterday was get a strep test that came back negative without any follow-up yet. I don't know if I shouldn't be seeing people in this state. I don't know for how long I should be cautious for. I just watched an Instagram reel where two women who are audhd were talking about the exhaustion of working at a full time job in a corporate office not because of physically being there, although that doesn't help given all the sounds, lights, smells and just having to be there for 8 hours but more specially because of the transition to the office. The getting there makes them feel miserable. It made me think about my daily life in high school and how exhausted I was because I actually did want to leave our apartment so I didn't have to be at home. But there's no where safe for a young girl to be alone in the city. And so I just played the role of going to school for everyone else. I'd tire myself out with having to get up at 6 am to get on the train around 7 so I could be at school around 8am every day. And then do it all over again in the afternoon. And then do homework. And have nothing to be joyful about. 

Now I think about how I stay at home all the time. I've thought about going in more. But it makes me anxious because every time I go into the office just once a week, it's already such a challenge. And really it's all the mental gearing up for driving, temperature changes, worrying about eating, the music I can't listen to when I'm there. I don't have habits and it's not like they're ever going to stick as a habit naturally without me trying to convince myself that I have to brush my teeth, and take a shower, and put on some clothes that are uncomfortable and presentable. I hate having to just pretend all the time. Before the pandemic, I would take Lyft everyday and it felt great because I didn't have the mental load to make driving decisions in a short amount of time all before doing my day job of decisions. 

I still feel resentful that I was coerced into learning how to drive and that my anxiety and overwhelming mental labor wasn't good enough of a reason for his obsessive anxiety about money. I feel like I let him cross so many boundaries. He'd wear me down. And it was never enough. I feel so hollow sometimes now. I wish I was where I am right now without  betraying myself constantly. But I just wanted to feel safe. And this home was that until my dad passed. And now it feels meaningless and fake. I played a role. That's it.

journal:
I read this blog post after looking up the need to mirror all the time:

One of the biggest and most challenging aspects of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is often ‘The Chameleon Effect’ – or ‘mirroring’. This is the constant, unconscious change in the person’s ‘self’, as they struggle to fit in with their environment, or the people around them. It is, essentially, a fluctuating identity. It is the manifestation of a basic inability or difficulty in establishing a stable sense of self.

The presence of The Chameleon is often one of the main obstacles to effective initial treatment and diagnosis of BPD, as it affects the interaction between patient and doctor, and can mask the disorder itself. It also affects and masks the way in which BPD intersects with other disorders that may have developed in connection with it – creating a complex web of behaviours that can be hard to untangle. The irony is that, without diagnosis and treatment, most are unaware of The Chameleon, and it is only through awareness that The Chameleon can be managed.

Though I was diagnosed some time ago, and am now (relatively) successful at managing my BPD, I am only recently getting to know my Chameleon. BPD and its insidious brethren are ugly, unpleasant and unsettling things to deal with and perhaps it is the case that my mind slowly processes them at a pace it knows to be comfortable and realistic for me. Accepting the fact of BPD is one thing, but admitting to the presence of The Chameleon truly slices to the core of all of that pain and insecurity – all of which is like pouring acid on an already gaping wound, for an emotionally dysregulated Borderline.

Now that I am acknowledging the presence of my Chameleon, I am beginning to wonder if this is actually the key to everything. The whole kit and caboodle. The crux of the issue. From what I can see, everything stems from this lack of a stable self. People with Borderline Personality Disorder instinctively ‘mirror’ to fit in, because without that behaviour, we have no idea what will happen. We have little or no sense of our own identity, so we can’t know if that will be acceptable to others. Without acceptance by others, we risk abandonment, which is often an intense fear for Borderlines. Why do we have this intense fear of abandonment? Because if we are abandoned, we have nobody to ‘mirror’. The fear of abandonment is a fear of being alone. It is terrifying to be left alone with yourself, when you don’t know who yourself is.

Imagine being entirely alone, looking into a mirror, and seeing a total stranger. Or, worse still, seeing nobody at all. There is no ‘you’. That’s kind of horrifying, right? So you’ll go to great lengths to avoid that situation, because, as an emotionally dysregulated person who experiences feelings in extremes, that situation will put you headfirst into a tailspin.

Now, I feel as though I have almost finished this monster of a jigsaw puzzle. I am close to seeing the big, completed picture. Perhaps this explains the terrifying, recurring, childhood nightmares featuring facelessness. It explains the debilitating childhood fear of being alone – so intense it caused hallucinations (externalisation of anxiety). It helps explain why, as an adult, I regularly experience severe dissociation. It explains further why the coping mechanisms that have developed over time – such as OCD – mainly serve as attempts to exert control over external daily life, as internally there is chaos.

It also explains why I am regarded by others as something of a ‘social butterfly’, constantly flitting from group to group, person to person, being different things to different people, as required. It explains my inability to say “no”. It explains why my persona changes depending on whom I interact with – even down to my accent and mannerisms. These are not conscious behaviours, but I have become more aware of them over time. I have begun to catch my Chameleon in action.

This is all good progress for me, as it is soothing to have explanations and answers. But mostly, it provides hope for lasting recovery. If the central problem is an unstable sense of self, the answer must be to build a more stable one. I just have to figure out how. I believe I have started to lay the foundations, and I am incredibly lucky to have people in my life that are willing and able to see beyond my Borderline Personality Disorder. I’m under no illusions, however – this is a chronic illness and I will never be free of it. But I can have enough awareness to keep it at a low, manageable level. The next step is to continue working towards a stable self that I can have confidence in. Only then can I can tame my Chameleon.

Have I finally reached the pot of explanation at the end of my enormous psychological rainbow? I’m not entirely sure, but the ground certainly seems to be solidifying beneath my feet.

journal:
My Dual-Path Escalator Framework

⸻

The Floor: Non-Negotiables

(applies to every relationship, no matter the type)
	•	Conflict engagement
“I need someone who doesn’t avoid conflict or leave me to carry the weight of it alone. Even if it’s uncomfortable, I need them to step in with me and actually work through things.”
	•	Accountability
“I need someone who can admit when they’ve hurt me or made a mistake, and not shift blame or pretend it didn’t happen. Owning actions is essential if I’m going to feel safe with them.”
	•	Boundaries
“I need someone who accepts my boundaries as a given, not as something to argue against or test. Respecting where I draw lines is a baseline for trust.”
	•	Respectful communication
“I need someone who listens to my needs and feelings without minimizing them or reducing me to a problem to solve. Being dismissed erodes safety for me.”
	•	Dignity
“I need to be met in ways that protect my dignity, especially when I’m vulnerable or when things are hard. Even in conflict or moments of failure, how I’m treated matters as much as what’s said.”

⸻

Path A: Romantic/Sexual Escalator

Step 1: Sexual Connection

“Sex on its own isn’t enough to move upward. But if it’s present, I need it to be about mutual trust and safety — not performance or obligation. If there’s no safety in how sex is handled, the relationship won’t go anywhere.”

Step 2: Preferred Qualities
	•	Curiosity and ambition
“I need someone who has a drive to explore and pursue what they’re curious about. I don’t want a partner who drifts through life without reaching for anything.”
	•	Nuance
“I need someone who seeks nuance instead of black-and-white thinking. I live in the gray areas, and I need a partner who doesn’t simplify or flatten complexity.”
	•	Leadership
“I need someone who wants to lead, but doesn’t do it at my expense. Leadership means initiative and direction, but it also means taking my feelings into account when making decisions.”
	•	Stability and security
“I need someone who feels grounded in their own skills and capabilities. If they’re relying on me for a sense of worth or direction, that feels unsafe to me.”

Step 3: The Ceiling (Romantic/Emotional Connection)

“If all of this is in place, then we can build the deeper connection: real intimacy, trust, shared values, and the willingness to be vulnerable with each other. That’s the ceiling of what I want in a romantic and sexual relationship.”

⸻

Path B: Platonic/Intimate Escalator

Step 1: Preferred Qualities (Without Sex)

“Not every deep relationship needs sex. Sometimes it’s the qualities — curiosity, nuance, leadership, stability — that form the foundation. These connections grow without sexual energy but are just as important.”

Step 2: The Ceiling (Platonic/Emotional Connection)

“The ceiling here looks very similar: intimacy, trust, shared values, and vulnerability. It’s about someone I can let into my inner world, who treats me with dignity, and who grows with me over time. It’s not less than a romantic bond — it’s simply a different form of depth.”

⸻

“For me, all relationships start with the same baseline of respect, dignity, and accountability. From there, some relationships grow through sex, others grow without sex — but both can climb the same escalator of qualities and emotional connection. What matters most isn’t whether it’s romantic, sexual, or platonic. What matters is how the person shows up and whether we can build dignity and trust together.”

Topics are tightly organized and consistently developed, language is precise and stable, and there are no unresolved contradictions; instead, the final paragraph explicitly integrates both paths into a coherent whole.
